title: Inference ops angles vs cloud-managed providers
summary: Working draft: concise messaging and technical rebuttals to position Redwood Inference against cloud-managed AI endpoints (AWS/GCP/Azure). Focus is on operational control, predictable economics, and smooth migration for platform and infra buyers.
key_customer_signals: Teams seeing unpredictable token spend after POC that breaks budgeting
Platform teams tired of opaque autoscaling charges from hyperscaler managed endpoints
Security/compliance owners demanding private control plane or VPC-isolated inference
SRE teams needing deterministic latency at 99th percentile for real-time features
ML engineers wanting stable model rollouts and verifiable metrics tied to eval sets
win_themes: Operational predictability: committed pools and billing transparency vs usage spikes in managed endpoints
Control plane sovereignty: private deployments and customer-managed keys where hyperscalers force multi-tenant control planes
Performance SLAs at scale: per-route latency guarantees and capacity planning for steady-state throughput
Cost-for-performance economics: batching, prefix caching, quantization guidance to reduce $/1000 tokens
Rollouts and regressions: model version pinning, canaries, automatic fallback to compatible variants
Observability built for inference: token-level cost traces, per-model error attribution, prompt-set regression alerts
Migration friction minimization: data plane compatibility, simple SDK swaps, and an actionable migration checklist
Regulated & air-gapped: on-prem/VPC options with KMS/HSM integrations and audit-ready logging
Operator-friendly defaults: pre-tuned batching/quantization profiles per workload to avoid long tuning cycles
competitor_notes: AWS SageMaker managed endpoints - Strengths: deep cloud integration (IAM, CloudWatch), enterprise contracts; Weaknesses: opaque per-request charges, limited private control plane options for inference, rollout ergonomics are clunky. Rebuttal: Redwood provides equivalent cloud-native integrations while offering predictable reserved capacity, clear per-token economics, and first-class rollout primitives.

GCP Vertex AI - Strengths: integrated MLOps stack and notebooks; Weaknesses: autoscaler heuristics can cause cost volatility, less emphasis on low-latency serving ops. Rebuttal: emphasize Redwood’s latency-tail SLA, inference-first runtime optimizations, and tooling to reduce surprise costs (batching/caching suggestions and recommendations).

Azure Managed/OpenAI-style endpoints - Strengths: developer familiarity, enterprise SSO and contracts; Weaknesses: vendor lock-in on model variants and limited on-prem/offline options. Rebuttal: pitch Redwood’s unified API that supports hosted, dedicated, and private deployments with model-variant fallbacks and easy migration paths.

Hyperscaler advantage pattern: they sell convenience (single bill, integrated identity, marketplaces) but operational cost transparency and deterministic performance at scale are often deprioritized. Counter: operational teams prefer explicit tradeoffs and measurable unit economics—our messaging should make that visceral (real numbers, not just claims).
battle_card_snippets: Objection: 'We already use managed endpoints and want to avoid another vendor.' Response: 'You can keep dev and storage in your cloud while moving inference serving to Redwood via simple SDK endpoint config — same developer ergonomics but with lower cost variability and stronger SLOs.'

Objection: 'Hyperscalers have better integrations.' Response: 'Redwood offers first-class integrations (IAM, KMS, VPC peering, logging sinks) and adds inference-specific hooks like token-level traces and cost allocation tags that hyperscalers don’t expose.'

Objection: 'We need air-gapped / on-prem.' Response: 'Redwood Private supports customer-controlled control planes and on-prem packages; we also provide migration runbooks and audit packaging to meet compliance gates.'

Technical TBD: latency at high QPS. Demo hook: 'show a 99th percentile latency graph for identical model/container running on Redwood Dedicated vs Vertex autoscaled endpoint under synthetic spike load.'
sales_pitch_lines: For platform eng: 'Stop paying surprises — reserve throughput, get clear token economics, and keep your existing cloud integration.'
For SRE: 'Predictable GPU pools + latency SLOs means you can set real uptime and tail-latency objectives for product teams.'
For ML infra lead: 'Model rollouts with canaries and automatic fallbacks reduces incident windows and lets you iterate safely.'
For procurement: 'Consolidated committed capacity and transparent per-token accounting simplifies forecasting compared to opaque autoscaler spikes.'
migration_playbook: 1) Audit current endpoints and usage patterns (top 10 routes by tokens/min and 99P latency).
2) Estimate committed capacity needed for baseline SLAs (use Redwood sizing template).
3) Set up a Dedicated pool and mirror a subset of traffic (shadowing/traffic-splitting).
4) Run metric parity checks (latency, throughput, output divergence on test prompts).
5) Switch gradually route-by-route while keeping fallback to original provider for 48–72h.
6) Post-migration: enable cost attribution tags and run a 30-day evaluation on token spend vs baseline.
success_metrics_to_track: Token cost variance (month-over-month) — target < 5% after reserved capacity tuning
99th percentile latency improvement or parity against previous provider
Number of rollback-free model rollouts per quarter (improve with Redwood canaries)
Operational MTTR for inference incidents — target 25% reduction in first 90 days
% of traffic on committed capacity vs burst — target > 70% after tuning
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: Procurement sees single-vendor risk. Mitigation: highlight multi-cloud compatibility and ability to run in customer VPCs / on-prem to reduce lock-in concerns.
Risk: Heavy lift to rewire CI/CD. Mitigation: provide SDK adapters, Jenkins/GitHub Actions templates, and a migration checklist with code snippets.
Risk: SRE concerns about another control plane. Mitigation: document control-plane telemetry, RBAC, and audit log retention options; offer on-prem control plane for high-regulation customers.
Risk: Model parity/regression. Mitigation: evaluation harness + deterministic compare step with canned prompts and diff tooling before cutover.

Which internal benchmarks should we use for demonstrating 99P latency under load for the sales demo kit?
Do we add a ready-made terraform module for customers to provision Redwood Dedicated in the same cloud account as their data? (Product + infra decision)

content:
Executive summary:
Redwood’s strongest counter to cloud-managed inference is operational clarity. Hyperscalers package convenience, but convenience frequently obscures cost and tail-latency tradeoffs. This doc lays out concise messaging for platform, SRE, ML infra, and procurement buyers, plus technical rebuttals and a concrete migration playbook.

Principles to lean on in messaging:
- Make economics tangible: use $/1000 token comparisons and show committed vs burst spend on typical workloads.
- Show tails, not just averages: product owners care about 99P latency incidents.
- Reduce perceived vendor surface: emphasize integrations and ability to run in-customer clouds.
- Operationalize trust: highlight model rollouts, canaries, and rollback safety nets.

Example demo flows and data points to include in sales collateral:
- Side-by-side chart: token cost vs QPS for a 4k-context LLM comparing managed autoscale vs Redwood Dedicated with reserved capacity.
- Canary demo: deploy a model variant to 5% traffic and trigger a controlled regression; show automatic fallback in Redwood.
- Observability demo: token-level trace that attributes a spike to a mis-tuned prompt and the corresponding cost delta.

Appendix: Short scripts for SDRs and solutions engineers, a migration timeline, and internal owners for next steps.
notes: Draft tone intentionally pragmatic and technical — this is a working doc to iterate with SEs and Product. Avoid marketing hyperbole until we lock on pricing inputs from Finance.
